questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: The three missing-data mechanisms as a ladder
questions.learningObjective: distinguish completely random, ignorable and non-ignorable missingness
questions.stem: A survey has 12 per cent missing on an outcome, concentrated among respondents with the lowest income. The team writes that the data are missing at random because the missingness was not caused by the outcome itself. What is the right response?

options.text: It is missing at random if the chance of being missing depends only on recorded variables, so the claim holds only once the income variable is in the analysis model
It is completely random, because the missingness cannot be caused by an outcome that was never observed
options.misconception: treats an unobserved outcome as if it could not drive missingness

options.text: It is missing not at random, because concentrating the missingness in the lowest income group shows the process depends on an unobserved value
options.misconception: reads dependence on a recorded variable as dependence on an unobserved one

options.text: The mechanism is irrelevant, because an analysis that models the income variable is valid under all three mechanisms
options.misconception: claims modelling one covariate rescues a non-ignorable mechanism

questions.explanation: The three mechanisms form a ladder by what they assume about the missingness. Completely random missingness says the chance of being missing is unrelated to anything, observed or not, and it is the only one under which simply discarding incomplete records leaves an unbiased analysis. Missing at random says the chance of being missing depends only on variables the analysis has already recorded, which permits valid inference once those variables are in the model, even when the outcome itself would have predicted missingness had it been observed. Missing not at random says the missingness depends on the unobserved value itself, and nothing in the data can establish or refute that. The team's sentence is aiming at the second rung while the concentration in the lowest income group shows the missingness is at least related to something the analysis records. If income is in the model the position is defensible; if it is not, the wording has claimed more than the design supports.
questions.hint: Ask what the missingness depends on, not whether the outcome is a cause of it.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Overall missingness rate across unequal groups
questions.learningObjective: compute an overall missingness rate from two unequal groups
questions.stem: Group A contributes 1200 records of which 180 have a missing value, and group B contributes 1300 records of which 130 do. Compute the overall proportion of records with a missing value, to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: There are 180 plus 130, that is 310, missing records out of 1200 plus 1300, that is 2500, so the overall rate is 0.124. The two group rates are 0.15 and 0.1, and their simple average is 0.125, which is not the same number. The overall rate is a weighted average of the group rates, weighted by group size, and here group A holds 0.48 of the sample but 0.5806 of the missingness, so the pooled figure is pulled towards the group that over-contributes. That difference is small, 0.001, and it is small precisely because the two group rates are close. Where the rates diverge, the pooled figure and the average of the rates can differ enough to change a conclusion, and the pooled rate is the one that describes the study while the average of the rates describes nothing in particular.
questions.hint: Pool the missing counts and the record counts before dividing, rather than averaging two rates.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Complete-case analysis under two different mechanisms
questions.learningObjective: explain why discarding incomplete records is safe under only one mechanism
questions.stem: A longitudinal study loses 18 per cent of records at follow-up, and the loss is higher among participants with low baseline wellbeing. The analysis compares groups on the complete records and reports a difference. What is the correct account of that difference?

options.text: The difference mixes any effect of the follow-up with the fact that one baseline group was more likely to drop out, so its sign is not fixed by the design
The difference is unbiased, because the loss is concentrated in a group the analysis records, and a recorded difference is always correctable
options.misconception: treats a recorded cause of loss as automatically harmless

options.text: The difference is unbiased as long as the proportion lost is the same in both arms, whatever the mechanism
options.misconception: reduces the condition to a single overall rate

options.text: The difference is unbiased because the baseline measure was collected before the loss could occur
options.misconception: believes temporal order settles the selection problem

questions.explanation: Discarding incomplete records is unbiased only when being missing is unrelated to everything, observed or unobserved. Here the loss is concentrated in one measured group, so the surviving records over-represent the better baseline, and the comparison is made between samples that differed before the follow-up was lost rather than only because of it. The result is not necessarily biased in either direction, because the group with better baseline might have improved more, and the point is that its sign is not determined by the design. What rescues the analysis is the structure of the loss rather than its size: if missingness depends only on recorded variables, then modelling those variables on the complete records can recover the comparison, which is what multiple imputation is for. A large loss under a completely random mechanism is inconvenient, and a small loss under a non-ignorable one is unfixable.
questions.hint: Ask whether the records that disappeared differed from the records that stayed on something the analysis already knows.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Is missingness related to a fully observed covariate
questions.learningObjective: compute a chi-square statistic for missingness against a recorded covariate
questions.stem: Of 2500 records, 120 of the 1000 with low baseline severity have a missing value and 240 of the 1500 with high baseline severity do. Test whether missingness is associated with the severity stratum, and give the chi-square statistic on one degree of freedom, to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The two missing rates are 0.12 and 0.16. Under independence of stratum and missingness, the expected count in the low-severity missing cell is 1000 times 360 over 2500, which is 144.0, against 120 observed, and the corresponding high-severity expected count is 216.0 against 240. Summing the squared deviations over the expected counts gives 7.7882. A second route returns the same value: the two-proportion z statistic on the same table is 2.7907 and its square is 7.7882, which is the identity between the chi-square for a two-by-two table and the squared two-proportion statistic. The p value is 0.005259, so missingness is related to a covariate that was recorded in full. That is a useful finding rather than a bad one, because it means the missingness is ignorable given the recorded variables and can be modelled, and it is the first thing to check before deciding what to do about the loss.
questions.hint: Compute each expected count as its row total times its column total over the grand total, then sum the squared deviations over those expected counts.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: How far the missing would have to differ to explain a result
questions.learningObjective: solve for the gap among the missing needed to null a complete-case difference
questions.stem: Two arms of 100 each are compared. In the treated arm 60 records have an observed outcome with a mean of 0.70 and 40 are missing; in the untreated arm 60 have an observed mean of 0.40 and 40 are missing. Suppose the missing records in each arm share a common rate that differs by the same amount between the arms. Compute the complete-case difference and the size of the gap between the missing arms that would be needed for the full-sample difference to be zero, the missing in the untreated arm being the higher of the two, each to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The complete-case difference is 0.3. The full-sample difference is that figure weighted by the share observed, 0.6, plus the difference among the missing weighted by the share missing, 0.4, so setting the total to zero gives 0.6 times 0.3 plus 0.4 times the gap, and the gap is therefore minus 0.3 times 0.6 divided by 0.4, which is 0.45. A second route builds the two full-sample means directly: if the missing in the treated arm had a rate of 0.00 and the missing in the untreated arm 0.45, the treated mean is 0.42 and the untreated mean is 0.42, and those are equal. The number is large. A gap of 0.45 between the missing arms means the drop-out would have to be strongly related to the outcome in opposite directions in the two arms for the complete-case figure to be entirely an artefact, and a reader can judge whether that is plausible. This is the delta adjustment, and it is a range over a sensitivity parameter rather than a second estimate.
questions.hint: Weight the complete-case difference by the share observed and the missing difference by the share missing, and solve for the missing difference.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What ignorable missingness licenses
questions.learningObjective: state what a missing-at-random assumption permits and what it does not
questions.stem: A study's income variable is missing for 9 per cent of records, and the probability of being missing depends only on age and region, both of which are recorded. The team proposes multiple imputation using age and region. What does the assumption buy them?

options.text: It licenses drawing the missing values from their conditional distribution given the recorded variables, provided the imputation model can represent that distribution
It licenses discarding the incomplete records, because ignorable missingness is exactly the condition under which deletion is unbiased
options.misconception: confuses ignorability with a property of deletion

options.text: It licenses reporting the result without any interval, because the uncertainty about the missing values is small once the mechanism is known
options.misconception: turns an ignorability condition into a reason to drop the interval

options.text: It licenses treating the missing values as if they had been observed, because their conditional distribution is by construction the same as the observed one
options.misconception: conflates distributional equivalence with observed values

questions.explanation: The assumption says that once age and region are in hand, the chance of a missing income is unrelated to the income itself, and that is exactly what makes the imputation legitimate: values drawn from the conditional distribution given age and region are, on this assumption, draws from the right distribution rather than from a model of a different population. Two consequences follow and both are worth stating. The inference is valid provided the imputation model is flexible enough to represent that conditional distribution, which is the congeniality requirement, and a mis-specified imputation model reintroduces bias in a way that is easy to miss because the reported intervals will still look reasonable. And the assumption licenses the treatment of the missingness, not the possibility of bias elsewhere: a variable that was never measured is not rescued by any of this, and the analysis remains as vulnerable as ever to a relationship nobody recorded.
questions.hint: Ask what the assumption says about the missing values once the recorded variables are known.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Pooling across imputations
questions.learningObjective: compute the pooled variance from within- and between-imputation components
questions.stem: An analysis is run on 5 imputed data sets. The five estimates are 0.30, 0.34, 0.28, 0.32, 0.31 and the five within-imputation variances are 0.0090, 0.0098, 0.0087, 0.0093, 0.0091. Compute the total variance of the pooled estimate, which is the average within-imputation variance plus one plus one over the number of imputations times the between-imputation variance.
questions.explanation: The pooled estimate is the mean of the five, 0.31, and the average within-imputation variance is 0.00918. The between-imputation variance is the sum of the squared deviations from that mean divided by one fewer than the number of imputations, which is 0.0005. The total variance adds that to the within-imputation average scaled by one plus one over five, giving 0.00978, and the standard error of the pooled estimate is the square root, 0.0989. The two components answer different questions. The within-imputation part is the ordinary sampling error, as if the completed data were real, and it would be the whole story if the imputations all gave the same answer. The between-imputation part is the price of not knowing the missing values, and it is why the pooled interval is wider than any single analysis would report. A five-imputation set whose estimates differ by a few hundredths carries little between-imputation variance, and the total is close to the average within-imputation variance.
questions.hint: The between-imputation variance divides the squared deviations by one fewer than the number of imputations, and the total adds it scaled by one plus one over that number.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Fraction of missing information
questions.learningObjective: compute the fraction of a pooled variance due to imputation
questions.stem: An imputation analysis uses 5 data sets. The average within-imputation variance is 0.00918 and the between-imputation variance is 0.0005. Compute the fraction of missing information, which is one plus one over the number of imputations times the between-imputation variance divided by the total variance, to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: One plus one over 5 is 1.2, and 1.2 times 0.0005 is 0.0006, which is the inflation the between-imputation variance contributes to the total. The total variance is that figure added to 0.00918, namely 0.00978, and the fraction is 0.0006 over 0.00978, which is 0.0613. A second route returns the same number from the total directly: the fraction is the excess of the total over the within-imputation average divided by the total, that is 0.0006 over 0.00978, and those two expressions are the same quantity written two ways. A fraction of about six per cent says that roughly six per cent of the uncertainty in the pooled estimate is attributable to not knowing the missing values rather than to ordinary sampling, and the rest is sampling. The figure is the right one to quote beside an imputation result, because it says how much of the interval is the analysis's own construction, and a result whose interval is almost entirely imputation-driven deserves a different kind of scepticism from one where the loss is negligible.
questions.hint: Divide the scaled between-imputation variance by the total, or equivalently the excess of the total over the within-imputation average by the total.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Why the degrees of freedom are not the complete-case count
questions.learningObjective: explain why an imputation analysis reports fewer degrees of freedom than the complete-case analysis
questions.stem: A two-group analysis on 100 complete records reports 98 degrees of freedom. The same analysis run on 5 imputed data sets reports a much smaller adjusted figure. A reviewer asks why imputing more data has reduced the available information. What is the right answer?

options.text: The completed records supply information but the variation across imputations must also be estimated, and the degrees of freedom spent on that come out of the count the completed data appear to offer
The count is wrong and should be raised, because the incomplete records were used and every used record adds a degree of freedom
options.misconception: counts used records as if using them were free

options.text: The count is unchanged at 98, because the degrees of freedom depend on the sample size and the imputation method does not change the sample size
options.misconception: ignores that the method changes what has to be estimated

options.text: The count should be 100 rather than 98, because the two-group comparison spends one degree of freedom rather than two
options.misconception: misstates how a two-group comparison spends degrees of freedom

questions.explanation: The complete-case analysis throws the incomplete records away and then spends its remaining degrees of freedom on the contrast it cares about, and reporting 98 is honest about that restricted analysis. The imputation analysis recovers the information in the incomplete records but cannot claim it as free: the pool of estimates varies across the imputations, and the between-imputation variance is the part of the uncertainty that comes from the fact that the missing values were never known. Some of the degrees of freedom the completed data appear to supply are consumed by estimating that spread, which is why the adjusted count falls below 98 even though more records entered the analysis. This is a real cost and not a technicality. The two numbers are answering different questions, the complete-case one about the records that survived and the adjusted one about the analysis that was actually run, and a report that quotes 98 for an imputation analysis is claiming precision the method does not deliver.
questions.hint: Ask where the extra records came from and what had to be estimated along with them.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Adjusted degrees of freedom for an imputation analysis
questions.learningObjective: compute an adjusted degrees-of-freedom count for a pooled imputation estimate
questions.stem: An imputation analysis pools 5 data sets. The fraction of missing information is 0.0613 and the complete-case analysis had 98 degrees of freedom. The large-sample degrees of freedom are one fewer than the number of imputations times one plus one over the fraction of missing information, all squared, and the adjusted count is one more than that divided by one plus three over the complete-case count. Compute the adjusted count, to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The first stage is four times one plus one over 0.0613, all squared. One over 0.0613 is 16.3, so the bracket is 17.3 and the square gives 1197.16. The second stage adds one to that and divides by one plus three over 98, which is one plus 0.0306, so the adjusted count is 78.6911. The comparison that matters is with the 98 the complete-case analysis would have reported. The adjusted figure is below it, and that is the honest answer: the analysis used more records and knows less about the precision of its own result, because the between-imputation spread had to be estimated from only 5 values. The gap narrows as the number of imputations rises, and with 24 imputations the adjusted count is 93.9864 rather than 78.6911, a recovery of 15.2954 degrees of freedom, which is the practical reason for the recommendation to use a decent number of imputations rather than three.
questions.hint: Square the bracket, add one, then divide by one plus three over the complete-case count.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Weighting observed records by their probability of being observed
questions.learningObjective: compute a weighted mean that corrects for differential loss
questions.stem: Two groups of 600 records each are followed up. 500 records in group A were observed and 470 in group B, with mean outcomes of 7.2 and 6.0 respectively. The overall observed rate is 0.78 and the observed rates within the groups are 0.84 and 0.72. A stabilised weight for a record is the overall observed rate divided by the observed rate of its own group. Compute the two weights and the weighted mean of the observed outcomes, to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The stabilised weights are 0.78 over 0.84, which is 0.9286, and 0.78 over 0.72, which is 1.0833. Group B was less likely to be observed, so its records carry the larger weight. Weighting the observed means by their record counts and the stabilised weights, and dividing by the total weight, gives 6.5723. The unweighted mean of the observed records is 6.6186, so the correction moves the figure by -0.0462. The two routes to the weighted mean are the same calculation written as a ratio of weighted sums and as a weighted average, and they agree exactly. The method replaces the discarded records with large weights on the surviving ones, which is legitimate when the probability of being observed is related only to recorded variables, because the weights then reconstruct the composition the full sample would have had. Where that probability also depends on something unrecorded the weights cannot repair it, and the estimate inherits the same problem the complete-case analysis had, in a form that is harder to see because the numbers still look tidy.
questions.hint: Multiply each group's observed mean by its record count and its weight, then divide by the total weighted count.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Why a not-at-random mechanism cannot be tested
questions.learningObjective: explain why a non-ignorable missingness mechanism escapes the data
questions.stem: A study's outcome is missing for patients whose illness was severe at the point of discharge. A reviewer notes that the analysis cannot distinguish this from the alternative that the outcome is missing for patients whose illness was mild. What is the right reading?

options.text: Both stories predict the same observed records, so no analysis of this data set can separate them and the response is to state the range of missing values that would change the conclusion
The two stories can be separated, because the clinician who recorded the discharge severity also recorded why the follow-up was missed
options.misconception: invents an auxiliary record that the design does not contain

options.text: The two stories can be separated, because the missingness rate is higher for severe illness and that is itself evidence for the first story
options.misconception: treats the pattern that fits both stories as discriminating between them

options.text: The mechanism can be tested by comparing the complete records with a sample of patients whose outcome was recovered from notes
options.misconception: describes a validation subsample that would require data the study lacks

questions.explanation: The two mechanisms make opposite predictions about exactly the records that are absent, so the data contain no information that separates them. Whatever comparison the study makes, the observed records can be produced by either story, and the analyst has one data set and two equally good explanations of it. This is a genuine limit rather than a failure of technique, and it is why the response is a sensitivity analysis rather than a test: the analyst states what the missing values would have to look like for the conclusion to change, and reports the range. What the study can do is reduce the size of the problem, by recording more about the state of the patient at the point the loss occurred, by following them up again, or by designing so that the outcome is observed whenever the covariate that drives the loss is. Those are design changes, and they are the reason the mechanism matters before the data are collected rather than after.
questions.hint: Ask what the absent records would have to contain for the two stories to look different.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Complete-case against covariate-adjusted comparison
questions.learningObjective: compare a complete-case difference with an adjusted and a full-sample difference
questions.stem: A study has 400 records per treatment arm with a baseline stratum. In the low stratum each arm has 200 records with 60 outcomes untreated and 100 treated. In the high stratum each arm has 200 records with 120 outcomes untreated and 160 treated. A baseline covariate is recorded for all of the low stratum, for 100 of the high-stratum untreated records and for only 20 of the high-stratum treated records. Compute the complete-case risk difference and the risk difference among all records, each to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: Among the complete cases the untreated arm has 300 records with 120 outcomes and the treated arm 220 with 116, so the complete-case risk difference is 0.1273. Among all records each arm has 400 records with 180 outcomes and 400 with 260, giving 0.2. The complete-case figure is 0.0727 below the full-sample one. The cause is visible in which records survived: the treated arm kept 20 of its 200 high-stratum records and the untreated arm kept 100, so the complete-case sample is built almost entirely of low-stratum treated records, which have the better outcome. The covariate-adjusted difference on the same complete records, obtained by weighting the two stratum-specific differences by stratum size, is 155.034, which returns the full-sample value. That agreement is the point: under a mechanism in which the loss depends only on the recorded stratum, adjusting on the stratum recovers the comparison that discarding the records destroyed.
questions.hint: Compute each arm's risk from its own totals, then subtract; then check that the stratum-weighted difference returns the full-sample figure.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Sequence for an imputation analysis
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps of a multiple-imputation analysis
questions.stem: A team has a dataset with 15 per cent of records missing on two variables and has decided to use multiple imputation. Put these steps in the order they should be carried out.

options.text: State the estimand and the variables in the analysis, since these determine what the imputations have to represent
Choose a model for each variable with missingness that can represent its distribution given the analysis variables
Draw the imputations, recording the model and the seed so the set can be regenerated
Pool the estimates with the within- and between-imputation components, and report the fraction of missing information beside them
Re-estimate under a shifted assumption about the missing values and report the range over which the conclusion holds

questions.explanation: The order is the order of a research plan, because each of these decisions changes the answer and none of them can be revisited once the estimates are in front of the analyst. Specifying the estimand comes first, since what is being estimated determines which variables must be in the imputation model and therefore how much the imputations matter. Choosing a model for each variable with missingness comes next, and the requirement is that it be able to represent the conditional distribution given the variables in the analysis, which is what makes the draws congenial with the analysis that follows. Drawing the imputations is mechanical once the first two steps are done. Pooling comes last and is a fixed set of arithmetic that adds nothing to the judgement and everything to the correctness, since the between-imputation variance has to enter the interval. Sensitivity to the assumed mechanism belongs alongside the pooling rather than instead of it, because a single pooled result is only one point in a range that the assumption defines.
questions.hint: Ask which of these steps is a decision rather than a calculation.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Expected number of imputed positives in a binary variable
questions.learningObjective: compute the expected count of imputed positives across an imputation set
questions.stem: Eight records have a missing binary variable. A fitted model of that variable on an observed covariate gives the probabilities of a positive value as 0.80, 0.65, 0.40, 0.15, 0.55, 0.90, 0.30, 0.70. Each record's value is drawn independently in each imputed data set. Compute the expected number of positive values across the eight records in one imputed data set, to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The expected count is the sum of the eight probabilities, which is 4.45, and a second route gives it as eight times their average, which is the same figure. The expected number of negatives is 3.55. The realised count will differ from 4.45 in any particular imputation, and the spread of that count across an imputation set is the square root of the sum of the probability times one minus the probability, which is 1.2298, so an imputation set of a handful of data sets will show counts varying by about that much around the expectation. That variation is not a defect of the method and it must not be suppressed: it is the mechanism by which the uncertainty about the missing values enters the analysis, and the between-imputation spread is computed from precisely these draws. A team that reported the expected count as though it were an observed count would be reporting a property of its model rather than a property of its data.
questions.hint: Add the eight probabilities; equivalently multiply their average by eight.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What congeniality of the imputation model requires
questions.learningObjective: state what it means for an imputation model to match the analysis model
questions.stem: The analysis regresses the outcome on a treatment indicator and a continuous covariate, and the imputation model for the outcome regresses it on the same two. The analysis allows a curved relationship with the continuous covariate and the imputation model does not. A reviewer raises this. What is the concern?

options.text: The imputation model cannot represent a relationship the analysis allows, so the completed records carry a bias the reported interval will not reflect
There is no concern, because both models contain the treatment indicator and the covariate, which is what the requirement asks for
options.misconception: reduces congeniality to variable membership alone

options.text: The analysis should be changed instead, because an analysis that allows a curved relationship cannot be validly imputed
options.misconception: reverses which of the two models has to adapt

options.text: The concern disappears once the number of imputations is raised, because more draws will eventually include curved values
options.misconception: believes more draws repair a mis-specified conditional model

questions.explanation: The two models have to be able to agree about the conditional distribution for the combination to carry its intended meaning, and here they cannot: the analysis can represent a curved relationship that the imputation model cannot, so the values drawn for the incomplete records are drawn from a distribution the analysis does not use. The consequence is not that the estimates are necessarily badly biased, since with a modest amount of missingness the two will often land close together, but that the bias has no sign and no bound the analyst can state, and the reported interval will not cover it. The requirement is usually described as the imputation model needing to include every variable in the analysis model, to use the same functional form, and to include interactions the analysis uses. It is a requirement on the imputation model rather than on the analysis, and the cheaper repair is to enrich the imputation model rather than to simplify the analysis.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two models can represent the same conditional mean.

questions.topic: Degrees of freedom lost by using too few imputations
questions.learningObjective: compute the degrees-of-freedom cost of a small imputation set
questions.stem: A dataset has 24 per cent of its records with at least one missing value, and the guidance is to use at least that many imputations. The fraction of missing information is 0.0613 and the complete-case analysis had 98 degrees of freedom. The analysis used 5 imputations instead. Compute the adjusted degrees of freedom at 24 imputations and at 5, and give the difference, each to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: At 24 imputations the large-sample count is 23 times one plus one over 0.0613 squared, and the adjusted count is 93.9864. At 5 the corresponding figures are 1197.16 and 78.6911. The loss from using 5 rather than 24 is 15.2954 degrees of freedom, against the 98 the complete-case analysis would have had. The reason the cost is real is that the between-imputation variance is estimated from the spread of the 5 estimates, and a spread computed from five values is itself imprecise, so the interval that is supposed to absorb the uncertainty about the missing values is built on a noisy estimate of that uncertainty. The size of the loss is modest here, and it grows with the fraction of missing information: the more of the result depends on the imputations, the more the count of imputations matters. That is why the recommendation scales with the proportion of incomplete records rather than being a fixed number.
questions.hint: Recompute the adjusted count at each number of imputations and subtract.

questions.topic: A value the participant actually gave
questions.learningObjective: state what should happen to a value that was recorded but unusable
questions.stem: A participant's response of 999 to an item whose scale runs from 1 to 10 is recorded in the raw data and the instrument's documentation says 999 was used to mean not applicable. A colleague proposes deleting the record. What is the right response?

options.text: It is a deliberate code whose meaning is documented, so the record is recoded under the instrument's rules and the recode is recorded rather than the record deleted
It is an outlier, so the record should be deleted because a value outside the scale cannot be used in any form
options.misconception: treats a documented code as an unusable observation

options.text: It is missing data, so the record should be dropped from the analysis of that item and retained for the other items
options.misconception: assumes a documented substantive code is a refusal

options.text: It should be recoded to the scale midpoint, because a value outside the range still has to sit somewhere in the analysis
options.misconception: invents a recode that biases the value toward the centre

questions.explanation: The record is not missing and it is not an outlier, it is a value the instrument deliberately used to record a state the scale cannot express, and the documentation says so. That makes it a recoding decision, and recoding decisions are made by applying the instrument's own rules and then recording what was done, not by deleting observations. Deleting the record discards the participant's answers to every other item along with the one unusable response, which is a cost paid for a problem that a single recode solves. Converting the value to missing, on the other hand, is defensible only if the instrument's rule is that 999 is a refusal rather than a substantive answer, and that is a different claim from the one the documentation makes. The general point is that three states are easily confused: not asked, asked and declined, and asked and given a value that falls outside the scale. Each needs a different code, and the code belongs in the data dictionary before the analysis rather than in a cleaning script afterwards.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Deterministic regression imputation deflates the variance
questions.learningObjective: compute the variance left after completing a variable by its prediction
questions.stem: A variable is completed by predicting it from a covariate, with no residual added, using a coefficient of 0.6 and a covariate variance of 20.0. The true variance of the variable is 10.0. Compute the variance of the completed data and the resulting correlation between the two variables in the completed sample, each to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: Completing a record with its prediction puts no residual variation into the filled values, so the completed variable carries only the variation the covariate can explain. The variance of the predictions is the square of the coefficient times the covariate variance, that is 0.6 times 0.6 times 20.0, which is 7.2 against a true variance of 10.0. The deflation factor is 0.72, so two and a bit tenths of the variable's variance has simply been removed. The correlation is the damaging part: the covariance with the covariate is the coefficient times the covariate variance, and dividing that by the square root of the completed variance times the covariate variance gives a correlation of 1.0, that is a perfect one. A deterministic completion therefore manufactures a perfect association out of a data-generating process in which the true correlation was 0.8485. This is why imputation draws a value rather than computing one, and why the rule that the imputed values must carry genuine variability is not a formality.
questions.hint: The completed variance is the coefficient squared times the covariate variance, with no residual term added.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Completing the data against analysing the available data
questions.learningObjective: check that completing and analysing the records reproduces the available-data slope
questions.stem: Eight records have a covariate observed for all of them, and the outcome is observed for six of them with a slope of 1.9771 on the covariate. The outcome is then imputed for the remaining two, drawing from the fitted regression conditional on the covariate. Averaging the fitted slope over 4000 completed data sets gives a value very close to the complete-case slope. Report the complete-case slope, the average slope across the completed data sets, and the standard deviation of that slope across the sets, each to four decimal places.
questions.explanation: The complete-case slope is 1.9771. Refitting on each completed data set and averaging over 4000 of them gives 1.9773, which differs from the complete-case figure by 0.0001. The agreement is not a coincidence and it is a known result: for a linear model with a single predictor, the complete-case slope is the solution to the same estimating equations that the completed data satisfy in expectation, so the imputation recovers it. The quantity that does differ is the precision. The spread of the slope across the completed sets is 0.0169, against a complete-case standard error of 0.0398, and the larger figure is the honest one, because it includes the uncertainty about the two values that were never observed. So completing the data recovers the estimate and not the interval, and any analysis that reports the complete-case precision alongside an imputation estimate is quoting a number for a question the data cannot answer.
questions.hint: Average the fitted slopes across the completed data sets and take their standard deviation; the estimate should reproduce the complete-case slope.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What pooling across imputations averages
questions.learningObjective: state what the pooled estimate combines and what it does not
questions.stem: An analysis has produced 5 estimates and 5 variances and pools them. A colleague proposes reporting only the average of the 5 estimates and discarding the variances because the estimates are close. What is the right response?

options.text: The disagreement among the five estimates is the only evidence about the unobserved values, so discarding the variances reports the imputation as if it had found the answer rather than bracketed it
The variances can be discarded, because the five estimates are computed from the same records and so carry no information about one another
options.misconception: assumes shared records make the estimates identical

options.text: The variances can be discarded, because the average of five estimates is more precise than any one of them and needs no interval
options.misconception: confuses averaging more draws with gaining information

options.text: The variances should be reported instead of the average, because the spread is a better estimate of the quantity than the mean of the estimates
options.misconception: prefers the dispersion over the central estimate

questions.explanation: The average of the estimates answers one question and the variances answer another, and both are needed. The average is the best single guess at the quantity, and it is what would be reported if the five estimates were five repeated measurements of something already known. They are not: they are five analyses of five different plausible completions of the same records, and the disagreement among them is the only information the study has about the values that were never observed. Discarding that disagreement reports the imputation as though it had found the answer rather than as a set of draws around it, and the interval that comes out is the interval of a single analysis repeated five times, which is narrower than the uncertainty actually is. The pooled variance is built precisely to add the spread of the estimates to the ordinary sampling error, and the fraction of missing information derived from it is the number that tells a reader how much of the reported uncertainty is the analyst's own construction.
questions.hint: Ask what the disagreement among the five estimates is evidence about.

questions.topic: What multiple imputation cannot repair
questions.learningObjective: state the class of problem that imputation leaves untouched
questions.stem: A study has 20 per cent of its outcome missing, and a multiple-imputation analysis is planned using age, sex and region. The team adds that the analysis will now be free of bias. What is the right response?

options.text: Only the loss of records is addressed, so an unmeasured confounder, a loss that depends on the unobserved outcome, and a variable never collected are exactly as much of a problem as before
All bias is removed, because drawing the missing values from a fitted model supplies the information the records would have carried
options.misconception: claims a model recovers information that was never collected

options.text: Only the loss of records is addressed, and a measured confounder that is itself missing is handled because the analysis includes it
options.misconception: claims a partially missing confounder is fully handled

options.text: The analysis is unbiased provided the imputation model contains every variable in the analysis, and no other condition is required
options.misconception: states the congeniality requirement as sufficient for validity

questions.explanation: The analysis is free of bias from one thing only: the loss of records, and only under the condition that the probability of being lost depends on nothing beyond the three recorded variables. Everything else the design is exposed to is exactly where it was before. A confounder that was never measured is not in the imputation model, so drawing the missing outcomes from the model does not break the route it creates. A variable that is missing for a reason that depends on the unobserved outcome itself is not repaired by drawing from a conditional distribution, because the conditional distribution is the wrong one. And an instrument or an instrument-related quantity that was never collected cannot be reconstructed. The list of what imputation fixes and what it leaves alone is worth keeping in view, because the reportable claim is narrow: the estimate is no longer distorted by the records that are absent, and it is exactly as distorted as before by everything else.
questions.hint: Ask which of the threats to validity are in the imputation model and which are not.

questions.topic: How many imputations to estimate the spread between them
questions.learningObjective: solve for the number of imputations needed to estimate a between-imputation variance
questions.stem: The between-imputation variance is estimated from the spread of a small number of completed data sets, and its own relative standard error is approximately the square root of two over one fewer than the number of imputations. A relative standard error of 0.20 is wanted. How many imputations are needed, as an integer?
questions.explanation: Setting the square root of two over one fewer than the count equal to 0.20 and squaring gives two over one fewer than the count equal to 0.04, so one fewer than the count is two divided by 0.04, which is 50, and the count is 51. The check is that 2 over 50 is 0.04, whose square root is 0.20. The reason the requirement is so large is that this particular piece of the variance is estimated from a handful of numbers, and the cost of a small set falls on the one component that is supposed to quantify the uncertainty about the missing values. This is a different consideration from the recommendation to use at least the percentage of incomplete records, which is about the stability of the pooled estimate rather than the precision of the spread, and the two can point to different numbers. The formula is an approximation from the chi-squared distribution, and the practical reading is that a set of three or five data sets is enough to see whether the missingness matters and not enough to say precisely how much.
questions.hint: Square the target relative standard error, divide two by it, and add one.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Classical test theory and the true score
questions.learningObjective: state what a classical test theory decomposition asserts
questions.stem: A team's analysis plan says that each person's observed score equals their true score plus an error term, that the two are uncorrelated, and that repeated administrations of the measure draw from the same error distribution. What is being asserted?

options.text: That a score is a stable quantity about a person plus an occasion-specific error unrelated to that quantity, which is what makes a reliability coefficient meaningful
That a score is entirely occasion-specific, so two administrations of the same measure to the same person should differ substantially
options.misconception: states the opposite of the stable-component claim

options.text: That the error is proportional to the true score, so a reliability computed on high scorers differs from one on low scorers
options.misconception: describes a violation of the model as though it were the model

options.text: That repeated administrations are independent, so averaging administrations removes all error and yields the true score
options.misconception: conflates partial improvement with removing the error

questions.explanation: The decomposition is a model of what a score is rather than a claim about any particular study, and its two parts do different work. The additive form says the score a person obtains is a fixed quantity about them plus a fluctuation of the occasion, and it is what licenses the whole enterprise: a reliability coefficient, a standard error of measurement and a correction for attenuation are all consequences of it. The uncorrelatedness assumption says the error is unrelated to the true score, so a person with a high true score does not also tend to have a large error, and if it fails the reliability is not a single number for the whole sample. Both assumptions are idealisations. They are worth stating because the properties derived from them are routinely reported without them, and a reliability quoted as though it were a property of the instrument rather than of a model applied to it will be over-read.
questions.hint: Ask what the model treats as fixed about a person and what as varying with the occasion.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Reliability as a variance ratio
questions.learningObjective: compute a reliability coefficient from item and total variances
questions.stem: A scale has 20 items, each with a variance of 2.5, and the total score across the 20 items has a variance of 100. Compute the reliability of the total score as one minus the sum of the item variances divided by the total variance, to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The item variances sum to 20 times 2.5, which is 50, and one minus 50 over 100 is 0.5. The interpretation is that half of the observed variation in the total score is variation among people in the true quantity and half is error introduced by the occasion and the scoring. That ratio is also what licenses the two operations that follow from it. The standard error of a score is the score's own standard deviation times the square root of one minus the reliability, so an observed spread that is half error makes the standard error of a measurement just over seven tenths of the score's spread. And the reliability bounds the correlation that can be observed between this score and any other measure, because a correlation cannot exceed the square root of the product of the two reliabilities, so a scale at 0.5 cannot correlate with anything above about 0.71 however strong the underlying relationship. The number is a property of these items in this sample, not of the construct, and it is the reason a high score on a weakly reliable instrument carries less information than it appears to.
questions.hint: Sum the item variances, divide by the total variance, and take one minus the ratio.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Cronbach's alpha from an item table
questions.learningObjective: compute Cronbach's alpha from the number of items and their variances
questions.stem: A ten-item scale has item variances summing to 30.0 and a total score variance of 60.0. Compute Cronbach's alpha, which is the number of items over one fewer than that, times one minus the sum of the item variances divided by the total variance, to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The ratio of the item variances to the total variance is 0.5, so the bracket is 0.5, and ten over nine is 1.111111, giving 0.5556. Two features of the formula are worth separating. The bracket is the reliability as a variance ratio, and the factor of ten over nine is a correction that makes the figure behave sensibly as a function of the number of items rather than drifting below it. Alpha is a lower bound on the reliability of the composite under a specific set of assumptions about the item covariance structure, and it exceeds the simple variance ratio of 0.5 precisely because of that correction. The two figures are both defensible and they answer slightly different questions, which is why a report that quotes one of them without saying which is incomplete. Neither figure says anything about whether the items measure one thing.
questions.hint: Take one minus the ratio of the summed item variances to the total variance, then multiply by the number of items over one fewer than that.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Extending a scale with the Spearman-Brown formula
questions.learningObjective: predict the reliability of a longer form from a shorter one
questions.stem: A ten-item scale has a reliability of 0.6 and a second form of the same items is assembled with 20 items. Compute the predicted reliability of the 20-item form, to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The predicted reliability is the new number of items times the old reliability divided by one plus one fewer than the new number times the old reliability, which is 20 times 0.6 over one plus 19 times 0.6, giving 0.9677. The figure rises from 0.6 to 0.9677, and the reason is worth understanding rather than celebrating. Doubling the items cuts the error variance in half, since the errors are assumed uncorrelated across items, and it leaves the true-score variance unchanged, so the ratio of true to total improves. What the arithmetic also shows is diminishing return: the first few extra items do far more than the last few, and a scale at 0.97 has bought very little for a great deal of respondent time. The formula is a prediction under the classical assumptions and not a guarantee, since it assumes the added items are drawn from the same population as the original and are scored the same way, and an item that measures something else changes the composite rather than lengthening it.
questions.hint: The new reliability is the new number of items times the old, over one plus one fewer than the new number times the old.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a high alpha does not establish
questions.learningObjective: state the limit of a high internal consistency coefficient
questions.stem: A 14-item attitude scale returns an alpha of 0.89, and the report concludes that the scale is reliable and measures attitudes consistently across its items. A reviewer objects. What is the objection?

options.text: The coefficient says only that the items agree with one another, so a high value is equally consistent with a shared bias and a factor analysis is needed to show they share the intended construct
The objection is that alpha assumes the items are equally weighted, so an unweighted alpha overstates the reliability of a weighted composite
options.misconception: invents a weighting requirement the coefficient does not have

options.text: The objection is that alpha is only defined for scale data, so the coefficient is not interpretable for attitude items recorded on a five-point scale
options.misconception: rejects a coefficient that is defined for interval-scale responses

options.text: There is no objection, because internal consistency is the standard evidence that an instrument measures a single construct
options.misconception: confuses agreement among items with evidence of a single construct

questions.explanation: Internal consistency is about how much the items agree with one another and nothing about what they agree about. A set of items that all load on a second factor, or on a general factor of responding in a particular way rather than a particular attitude, will also produce a high coefficient, so the number is compatible with a scale whose items share a bias rather than a construct. What alpha does license is narrower and still valuable: that the errors of the items are small enough relative to the true-score variation that the composite carries real information, and that two administrations of the composite would agree more than two administrations of a single item would. The evidence that would address the reviewer's point comes from elsewhere: a factor analysis of the item responses, a check that the items behave the same across groups, and a demonstration that the composite relates to something outside itself in the way the construct predicts.

questions.topic: Standard error of a measurement
questions.learningObjective: compute the standard error of a single score from the reliability
questions.stem: An observed score has a standard deviation of 20.0 across a sample and the scale's reliability is 0.7. Compute the standard error of a measurement, that is the observed standard deviation times the square root of one minus the reliability, to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The standard error of a measurement is the score's own standard deviation multiplied by the square root of the share of its variance that is error. One minus 0.7 is 0.3, and the square root of that is 0.5477, so with a score standard deviation of 20.0 the result is 10.9545. Squaring it confirms the arithmetic from the other side: 20.0 squared times 0.3 is 120.0, whose square root is the same figure. The number is what it means that roughly two thirds of individual scores fall within about 10.9545 of the person's true score, so a difference between two people smaller than that cannot be read off their observed scores. That is the practical reason reliability is reported alongside a mean, and it is the reason a study that compares individuals on a weakly reliable scale has to design for larger differences than the construct would suggest. The figure is not a claim about how accurately the instrument was administered on any particular day.
questions.hint: Multiply the score's standard deviation by the square root of one minus the reliability, or take the square root of the score variance times that share.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Correcting a correlation for attenuation
questions.learningObjective: correct an observed correlation for the error in both variables
questions.stem: A correlation of 0.3 is observed between two measures whose reliabilities are 0.6 and 0.75. Compute the correlation the same two constructs would show if both measures were free of error, to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: Error in either variable drives an observed correlation towards zero, and the correction divides the observed correlation by the square root of the product of the two reliabilities, because the error variance in each measure is a fraction of the total variance in that measure and the two fractions multiply. The square root of 0.6 times 0.75 is 0.6708, and 0.3 divided by that is 0.4472. Two cautions belong with the figure. The correction is only meaningful up to the ceiling of 0.6708, because no correction can produce a correlation above what the reliabilities permit, and the corrected value here sits well inside that. And a corrected correlation is not a measurement of a different, truer relationship, it is a reconstruction of the relationship the classical model says lies behind the observed one, so it inherits every assumption the model makes. Reporting the correction without the ceiling beside it invites a reader to treat the result as a free improvement.
questions.hint: Divide the observed correlation by the square root of the product of the two reliabilities.

questions.topic: The ceiling a correlation cannot exceed
questions.learningObjective: compute the largest correlation two measures' reliabilities permit
questions.stem: Two measures have reliabilities of 0.6 and 0.75. Compute the largest correlation that could be observed between them however strongly the underlying constructs are related, to three decimal places.

questions.topic: A low test-retest figure
questions.learningObjective: interpret a test-retest reliability that is low by accident

options.text: The coefficient measures agreement over a week, so a low value is expected for a current-state construct and tells the design what change it could detect rather than showing the scale is faulty

questions.topic: Reliability of a composite from its parts
questions.learningObjective: compute a composite reliability from diagonal and off-diagonal terms
questions.stem: Four measures each have a reliability of 0.50 and the average correlation between any two of them is 0.20. Compute the reliability of their sum, as the sum of the diagonal terms plus twice the sum of the off-diagonal terms, divided by the number of measures plus twice the number of pairs times the average pairwise correlation.
questions.explanation: The diagonal terms sum to 2.0. There are four times three over two, that is 6, pairs, and at an average correlation of 0.20 they sum to 1.2, which enters twice, giving 2.4. The numerator is therefore 4.4. The denominator is the number of measures, 4, plus twice the number of pairs times the average correlation, which is 4 plus 2 times 6 times 0.20, that is 6.4. The ratio is 0.8462. The result is the point of combining measures at all: each has a reliability of 0.50 and the composite has one of 0.8462, because the errors of the four are less than perfectly shared while their true scores are positively related. The gain is smaller than it would be if the parts were independent, and it is smaller the more the parts overlap, so a composite of near-duplicate items adds little. The formula is the same quantity alpha estimates when the diagonal and off-diagonal terms come from a sample correlation matrix, which is why a table of item correlations and an item variance table will give the same answer for the same data.

questions.topic: Reliability of a difference between two measurements

questions.stem: Two measures have variances of 100.0 and 64.0 and a covariance of 40.0, with error variances of 40.0 and 24.0. Compute the reliability of the difference between them and the standard error of a difference, each to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The observed variance of a difference is the sum of the two variances less twice their covariance, which is 100.0 plus 64.0 less twice 40.0, that is 84.0. The error variance of a difference is the sum of the two error variances, 64.0, and the reliability is their ratio, 0.7619. The standard error of a difference is the square root of that error variance, 8.0. The result is counter-intuitive enough to be worth pausing on. Neither measure is very reliable, 0.6 and 0.625, yet the difference is more reliable than either, because the error in a difference is a sum rather than a single large quantity and because the positive covariance between the two measures cancels part of what remains. This is the statistical reason a within-subject design is more sensitive than a between-subject one, and it holds exactly when the two measures are positively correlated, as two measures of the same construct normally are. It also means a paired analysis can be the right choice for reasons of precision that have nothing to do with which comparison is more plausible.
questions.hint: The observed variance of the difference is the sum of the variances less twice the covariance; the error variance is the sum of the two error variances.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Differential misclassification of an exposure
questions.learningObjective: compute the odds ratio a misclassification scheme produces
questions.stem: A case-control study has 100 cases and 100 controls, and the true distribution is 80 exposed cases, 20 unexposed cases, 40 exposed controls and 60 unexposed controls, an odds ratio of 6.0. Reporting the exposure with a sensitivity and a specificity of 0.80 in both groups gives an odds ratio of 6.0. Now the cases are reported with a sensitivity and specificity of 0.80 and the controls with a sensitivity of 0.80 and a specificity of 0.90. Compute the odds ratio in the four reported cells, to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The reported cells become 64 exposed cases and 4 unexposed cases, and 32 exposed controls and 6 unexposed controls, so the odds ratio is 64 times 6 over 4 times 32, which is 3.0. The comparison that matters is with the non-differential scheme, which reproduced the true figure of 6.0 exactly. That is a real property and not an accident: when the exposure is misclassified at the same rate and to the same accuracy in cases and controls, the factors introduced cancel in the cross-product and the odds ratio is preserved. Change one of the four rates and they no longer cancel, and here the result is halved. Two cautions. The direction of the movement is not fixed in general, since it depends on which of the four rates differs and in which direction, and a differential scheme can inflate an association as easily as deflate it. And the analysis cannot detect the problem, because the reported cells are all it has; a differential scheme is invisible in the data and has to be addressed by design, by validation or by a record-linkage exercise.
questions.hint: Multiply each true cell by the relevant sensitivity or one minus the specificity, then take the cross-product ratio of the reported cells.

questions.topic: Regression calibration of an error-prone measure
questions.learningObjective: apply a calibration slope to an observed association
questions.stem: A validation subsample of 120 units is measured twice, once with an approximate instrument and once with a near-perfect one, and regressing the near-perfect measure on the approximate one gives an intercept of 0.4 and a slope of 0.82. The main study reports an association of 0.5 between the two constructs using the approximate instrument. Apply the calibration and report the corrected association, to three decimal places.

The same figure can be written as the calibration factor, one over the slope, which is 1.2195, multiplied by the association, and the two are the same operation. What calibration buys and what it costs are both worth stating. It corrects the attenuation that error introduces into a predictor, which is real and often large, and it does so with a slope estimated in a subsample where the truth is known. It corrects only that. The intercept in the calibration line reflects the mean of the true measure, so applying the line to a difference between groups moves the difference by a multiple of the slope while leaving the level alone, and a slope estimated in a subsample carries its own sampling error into every corrected figure. A simulation of the same validation design returns a slope near the stated 0.82, which confirms the figure is in the right range rather than pinning it exactly.
questions.hint: Evaluate the calibration line at the observed association; equivalently multiply by the calibration factor.

A random subsample of 200 is also measured with a near-perfect instrument, and the subsample is used to correct the cohort analysis. A reviewer asks what would have to be true for the correction to be valid. What is the right answer?

options.text: The subsample must be representative on the variables relating the error to the truth, the calibration must transfer across the range used, and its sampling error has to be carried into the corrected estimates
Nothing beyond the size of the subsample, because a random subsample is unbiased whatever the cohort looks like

options.misconception: reduces validity to a single agreement statistic

options.text: Only that the error is small, since a negligible error needs no correction and a large one cannot be corrected
options.misconception: assumes a large error is uncorrectable

questions.explanation: Three conditions, and they are not equally secure. The subsample has to be representative of the cohort on the variables that relate the error to the truth, and random selection is what buys that. The calibration line estimated in the subsample has to transfer, which in practice means the relationship between the approximate and the true measure has to be roughly the same across the range where the cohort analysis will apply it. And the analysis has to be willing to carry the subsample's own sampling error into every corrected estimate rather than treating the slope as known. A fourth condition is often left unstated: the corrected analysis assumes the measurement error is independent of the outcome given the covariates in the model, and a subsample that is only large enough to estimate a slope will not reveal a violation of that. questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What the bootstrap resamples
questions.learningObjective: state what a bootstrap estimate targets and what it assumes
questions.stem: A bootstrap is run by drawing 4,000 samples of 60 with replacement from an observed sample of 60 and refitting a median in each. A colleague says the resampling has removed the assumption that the sample is large enough for the estimate to be approximately normal. What is the right response?

options.text: It removes the normal approximation but keeps the requirement that the observed records represent the population, since every resample is drawn from those records
It removes every distributional assumption, because a resampling distribution is constructed from the data rather than from a model
options.misconception: claims the method is assumption-free

options.text: It removes the normal approximation and adds the assumption that 4,000 resamples is enough, which is a new cost rather than a saving
options.misconception: treats the resample count as a distributional assumption

options.text: It removes the normal approximation only for statistics that are already approximately normal, so the median gains nothing
options.misconception: restricts the method in a way that defeats its purpose

questions.explanation: The bootstrap replaces the normal approximation to the sampling distribution with the empirical distribution of the statistic computed on resampled records, and in that sense the normality assumption does go. What it does not replace is the assumption that the observed records are themselves a random sample from the population, because every resample is drawn from the sixty that exist rather than from the population. So the bootstrap is a statement about the sampling distribution of an estimator given this sample, and it inherits the design assumptions of the study rather than suspending them. Two further limits are worth naming. A statistic with no finite expectation, such as the sample maximum, has no usable bootstrap standard error however many resamples are drawn, which is the point at which the method's own logic runs out. And a percentile interval built this way inherits the skewness of the statistic, which is why a bias-corrected version exists.
questions.hint: Ask what population the resampled records are being treated as a sample from.

questions.learningObjective: compute a jackknife standard error from leave-one-out values
questions.stem: A sample has the six values 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13. Compute the jackknife standard error of the mean, as the square root of one fewer than the number of values over that number, times the sum of the squared deviations of the leave-one-out means from their own mean. Give the answer to four decimal places.
questions.explanation: Dropping each value in turn gives leave-one-out means of 9.0, 8.6, 8.2, 7.8, 7.4, 7.0, which average 8.0, and the full-sample mean is 8.0. The squared deviations sum to 2.8, and the jackknife standard error is the square root of five sixths of that, which is 1.5275. A second route gives the identical number: forming the pseudo-values, each being six times the full mean less five times the corresponding leave-one-out mean, yields 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, and their standard deviation divided by the square root of six is also 1.5275. The agreement between the routes is the check, and it is a special property of this statistic: for a mean the jackknife reproduces the textbook standard deviation of 1.5275 exactly, because the leave-one-out means lie on a straight line in the data. The jackknife earns its place for statistics where that is not true, and the demonstration that it agrees here is the reason to trust it where it is not.
questions.hint: Form the leave-one-out means, average them, and apply the jackknife variance formula; the pseudo-value route must return the same number.

Give each to three decimal places.

A second route confirms the standard error: building the pseudo-values from the leave-one-out medians and taking their standard deviation divided by the square root of nine returns the same 4.7971. The bias is the interesting part. It is not small, and it is negative, because removing a high value pulls the remaining median down and the leave-one-out values therefore sit below the median of the whole sample. That is a property of the median rather than a fault in the jackknife, and it is the reason a jackknife interval for a median is shifted from the estimate rather than centred on it. The jackknife is a good way to get a standard error for a statistic with no closed form and a poor way to get a bias correction for one whose leave-one-out values are not centred.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: The exchangeability a permutation test needs
questions.learningObjective: state the exchangeability a permutation test relies on
questions.stem: A permutation test labels every one of 40 records as treated or comparison in all possible ways and computes the difference in means for each. A colleague notes that the test assumes the labels could have been assigned any other way with the same likelihood. What is the right response?

options.text: The labels must be exchangeable under the null, which randomisation supplies and a rule-based assignment does not, so the resulting proportion is a tail probability only under that condition
No condition is needed, because enumerating every labelling is an exhaustive calculation and exhaustiveness replaces the exchangeability assumption
options.misconception: confuses an exhaustive computation with a valid reference distribution

options.text: The condition is that the two group sizes are equal, which the enumeration fixes and which is therefore the whole of the requirement
options.misconception: reduces the assumption to a balance the design already imposes

options.text: The condition is that the outcome is measured without error, since permutation tests are otherwise sensitive to measurement error
options.misconception: invents a measurement requirement the test does not have

questions.explanation: The requirement is that the labels be exchangeable under the null, and it is exactly the assumption randomisation buys and a non-randomised comparison does not. Under exchangeability every one of the possible labelings is equally likely if there is no association, so the proportion of them producing a difference as large as the observed one is a valid tail probability for the null, with no appeal to a distribution for the statistic at all. When the labels were assigned by a rule rather than at random, that symmetry is gone: the records that received one label differ systematically from those that received the other, and permuting the labels produces labelings that the design could not have generated, some of them more extreme than the observed one by a wide margin. The test then measures something, but not the null hypothesis it is named for. This is why a permutation test on an observational comparison is a descriptive summary of the data and not an inferential test of a causal claim.
questions.hint: Ask whether the observed labelling could plausibly have arisen from any of the others.

questions.topic: An exact permutation test on a small sample
questions.learningObjective: enumerate an exact permutation test and count the extreme labelings
questions.stem: Two groups of four each have values 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 4 and 2, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5. Give the proportion to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The observed difference in means is 0.3833. Of the 70 labelings, 2 produce a difference at least as large in absolute value, so the exact two-sided p value is 2 over 70, which is 0.0286. The count can be reasoned as well as enumerated: the eight values are consecutive integers, and the only way to split them into two fours whose means are as far apart as the observed split is to keep the four lowest together and the four highest together, with the two labelings that exchange the groups, which gives 2. The smallest value this exact procedure can return is one over 70, so with eight records no permutation test can produce a p value below 0.014 however large the difference, and that floor is a property of the sample size rather than of the data. It is the clearest argument for the exact procedure over an asymptotic one on small samples, where the normal approximation would happily report a p value the enumeration rules out.
questions.hint: Count the labelings whose absolute difference in means reaches the observed one, and divide by the total number of labelings.

questions.topic: A permutation test and a t test that disagree
questions.learningObjective: compare an exact permutation p value with the classical t test on skewed small data
questions.stem: Two groups of six have values 1.0, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5, 4.0 and 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5, 4.5, 20.0, the second group containing one value far from the rest. The observed absolute difference in means is 3.25. Compute the exact two-sided permutation p value over all 924 labelings, and report it to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: Of the 924 ways of choosing six of the twelve values for the first group, 276 give an absolute difference at least as large as the observed 3.25, giving 0.2987. The classical two-sample t test on the same data gives a t statistic of 1.1314 and a p value of 0.2843, and the two are close here. That closeness is the misleading part, because they agree for a reason that will not hold in general. The t test compares the observed difference with the spread of the difference under normality, and the single extreme value inflates both the observed difference and the spread that is supposed to calibrate it, so the statistic is pulled towards one and the p value upwards. A permutation test calibrates against the actual distribution of the statistic under label exchange, extreme values and all, which is why it is the safer choice on a small skewed sample. A companion case makes the point from the other side: on four clean values against four, the exact p value is 0.0286 against a classical 0.4601, and there the two are again close. Agreement between the two procedures is evidence that the normality assumption was harmless, not evidence that it was true.
questions.hint: Enumerate the labelings and count those reaching the observed difference; compare with the classical p value.

questions.topic: Clustering in the data and in the standard error
questions.learningObjective: explain what a cluster-robust variance corrects for and what it leaves alone
questions.stem: A study randomised 30 clinics and analysed 1,500 patient records with a model that includes an ordinary standard error. The records within a clinic share a clinician and a caseload. A reviewer recommends a cluster-robust standard error. What is the right response?

options.text: It corrects the standard error for the resemblance among records within a clinic, and it neither removes the resemblance across clinics nor fixes the small-cluster problem in its own estimation

It does not make the clusters independent of one another, so any feature shared across clinics, a common protocol or a common funding stream, still reduces the effective amount of information in a way the correction does not capture. And its own accuracy depends on the number of clusters, because the resemblance is estimated from 30 of them, so with a handful of clusters the correction is unreliable and the interval needs a smaller-sample adjustment.
