questions.topic: Asymptotic standard error of a sample median
questions.learningObjective: compute the asymptotic standard error of a sample median
questions.stem: A sample of 50 values is drawn from a normal distribution with standard deviation 3.0. Compute the asymptotic standard error of the sample median, to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The median of a sample converges at the rate of one over the square root of n times the inverse square root of four times the density of the sampling distribution at the population median, and for a normal distribution that density is one over sigma times the square root of two pi. The variance is therefore one over four n times that density squared, which simplifies to pi times sigma squared over two n, and with sigma of 3.0 and n of 50 the standard error is 0.5317. Two routes confirm it: the algebraic form and the expression sigma times the square root of pi over two n are identical, and a simulation drawing 4,000 such samples and taking the standard deviation of their medians returns 0.521. The practical figure to hold is the ratio to the standard error of the mean, which is the square root of pi over two, or about 1.25. A sample median is therefore about a quarter less precise than a sample mean from the same data, and a design that can afford a mean should not replace it with a median for convenience without costing itself a quarter of the sample size it needs.
questions.hint: The variance is pi times the population variance over two n, so the standard error is the population standard deviation times the square root of pi over two n.

It removes the influence of the aberrant record and also makes the fit robust to mis-specified functional form
options.misconception: adds a second repair the procedure does not provide

options.text: It is unnecessary, because the classical estimator already limits the influence of any one observation when the sample is large
options.misconception: denies that a single large value can move a fit

options.text: It will remove the finding, because a value of 900 indicates a recording error rather than a genuine case
options.misconception: presumes the aberrant value is an error

questions.explanation: A robust procedure bounds the influence any single observation can have on the estimate, which is exactly the right repair for one aberrant value: the fit changes little whether that record is present or not, and a classical fit would move substantially. What the procedure does not do is change the model. The relationship between the predictors and the outcome is still assumed linear in the coefficients, the predictors are still assumed free of the errors that would bias the slope, and the group means are still assumed to be what the design intended. A procedure that down-weights large residuals will also down-weight a genuinely unusual unit, and in a study where a rare case is the point, the remedy removes the finding. The pairing with a robust standard error matters as much as the estimator: fitting robustly and then reporting the classical standard error leaves the interval describing something the fit no longer is, and the two have to be chosen together.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the estimate when the aberrant record is deleted, and what the procedure assumes about the rest.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A Huber location estimate on a contaminated sample
questions.learningObjective: compute a Huber location estimate against the mean and the median
questions.stem: Seven observations are 0.4, 0.7, 0.9, 1.0, 1.2, 1.5, 12.0, six of them clustered near 1 and one of them at 12. Compute the ordinary mean, the median, and a Huber estimate that down-weights residuals beyond 1.345 times a scale taken as 1.4826 times the median absolute deviation, to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The mean is 2.5286, the median is 1.0 and the median absolute deviation is 0.3, giving a scale of 0.4448. Starting from the median and iterating a weighted mean in which an observation's weight falls to the inverse of its absolute residual once that residual exceeds 1.345 times the scale converges to 1.06. The mean is wrong by 1.5286 because one value carries a seventh of the total, the median is right, and the trimmed mean with the largest value removed is 0.95. The Huber estimate sits between the median and the clean cluster because it does not discard the extreme value, it discounts it, and that is the trade: a bounded-influence estimator keeps a record that is in fact informative while refusing to let it set the answer. The price is paid under the clean model, where a simulation of the same estimator on normal data gives a standard deviation of 0.1591 against 0.1644 for the mean, so the robust estimator gives up a little efficiency to buy its protection.
questions.hint: Iterate a weighted mean in which each weight is one inside 1.345 scale units of the current estimate and the inverse of the residual beyond it.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A trimmed mean and what it discards
questions.learningObjective: compute a trimmed mean against the ordinary mean
questions.stem: A sample of 11 values is 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 30. Remove 20 per cent of the observations from each tail, taking the count down to a whole number, and average what remains. Compute the trimmed mean, the ordinary mean and the median, each to three decimal places.
questions.explanation: Sorting the sample puts the largest value at the top, and 20 per cent of 11 is 2.2 which rounds down to 2 from each tail, so 2 observations are removed from the bottom and 2 from the top and 7 remain. The retained values sum to 19.0, giving a trimmed mean of 2.7143. A second route returns the same figure by subtracting the discarded sums from the total, which is 55.0 less 36.0. The ordinary mean is 5.0 and the median is 3.0, against a clean average of the ten uncontaminated values of 2.5. The gap between 2.7143 and 5.0 is the whole point: a single value of 30 among eleven observations is 27 per cent of the total, and no amount of extra records repairs a mean that has been moved that far. The cost is a real one, since 0.3636 of the data is discarded outright rather than down-weighted, so a trimmed mean is a good choice when contamination is expected and a poor one when the tails are informative.
questions.hint: Sort the values, drop the stated number from each tail, and average the remainder; the same figure comes from the total less the discarded sums.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Two analyses of one dataset, one robust
questions.learningObjective: appraise two analyses that differ only in their standard error
questions.stem: One dataset is analysed twice. The first analysis fits a linear model to 40 records whose error variance clearly grows with the predictor and reports a slope of 0.79 with a standard error of 0.18. The second reports the same slope with a standard error of 0.21 and adds a sentence saying the errors are not independent of the predictor. A draft reports the first. What is the defect?

options.text: The draft chose the standard error whose error assumption the data violate and did not disclose the choice, so the reader cannot see that the conclusion turns on which interval is reported
There is no defect, because the two standard errors are alternative estimators of the same quantity and either is acceptable
options.misconception: treats two intervals as interchangeable

options.text: The defect is that the second analysis adds a sentence about the errors, which signals doubt about the result unnecessarily
options.misconception: objects to disclosure of an assumption

options.text: The defect is that the slope is the same in both analyses, so the second analysis adds nothing and should not be reported
options.misconception: treats identical coefficients as evidence that nothing differs

questions.explanation: The two analyses fit the same model to the same records and therefore return the same coefficient, so the choice between them is entirely about the interval. The draft has picked the one whose standard error assumes an error structure the data visibly violate, which is the one that is too small. A slope of 0.79 with a standard error of 0.18 gives a t statistic near 4.4 and a p value well below 0.001, while the corrected version's 0.21 gives a t statistic near 3.8, and the difference between those two conclusions is a difference in a rounding of a standard error rather than a difference in evidence. Nothing in the draft discloses the choice, and a reader cannot recover it. The defect is not that the draft used the wrong standard error, which is an ordinary error, but that it used one without saying which and why, in a dataset where the choice was visible. The report should state the error structure it assumes, show the diagnostic that revealed the violation, and give the interval that follows from the structure the data support.
questions.hint: Ask what the two standard errors assume and which of those assumptions the data rule out.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: A claim resting on a normal-theory standard error
questions.learningObjective: identify the assumption a reported interval depends on
questions.stem: A report states that a coefficient of 0.42 has a standard error of 0.05, gives the interval as 0.32 to 0.52, and reports a chi-square of 70.4 on one degree of freedom. The dataset is 45 records and the residuals in a plot fan out with the size of the fitted value. A reader asks what the interval assumes. What is the right answer?

options.text: The interval is a normal-theory interval and its standard error pools the residual variance, which the fanning residuals make too small, so the interval is narrower than the evidence supports
The interval is sound, because a chi-square of that size is decisive whatever the residual pattern
options.misconception: treats a large statistic as independent of the assumptions behind it

options.text: The interval is unsound because 45 records are too few for any standard error to be meaningful
options.misconception: converts an assumption problem into a sample-size rule

options.text: The interval is sound provided the coefficient is reported as a proportion rather than a percentage
options.misconception: invents a units problem where none exists

questions.explanation: The interval is a normal-theory interval, and the quantity that is wrong about it is the standard error, not the coefficient. A chi-square of 70.4 on one degree of freedom is a large-sample statistic obtained by treating the standard error as the scale of a normal quantity, and the fanning residuals are exactly the pattern that makes that scale too small, because the high-fitted records contribute most of the residual variance and the pooled figure understates their uncertainty. The coefficient itself is not thereby wrong, since the violation concerns the spread of the errors rather than their mean, and a robust standard error on the same fit would usually leave the point estimate close. What changes is the interval, and with it the strength of the claim. A figure quoted to two decimal places with a chi-square to one invites a reader to treat the result as settled, and a diagnostic that plainly contradicts the assumption under which the interval was built is the kind of thing a report should raise itself.
questions.hint: Ask what the standard error pools, and whether the residuals make that pooling defensible.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Deciding between two analyses of a contaminated sample
questions.learningObjective: choose and justify an analysis for a dataset with a contaminated value
questions.stem: A cohort of 44 records has an outcome that is 900 in one record and ordinary elsewhere, and the predictor grows steadily across the sample. First say which features of the data threaten a conventional analysis, and then say what the report should contain.

options.text: The extreme value threatens the estimate and calls for a bounded-influence fit reported both with and without it, while the growing error calls for a standard error that does not pool the residual variance
Neither feature matters at 44 records, and the report should use the conventional fit with its textbook standard error and note that the sample is small
options.misconception: dismisses both features on the basis of sample size

options.text: Both features are the same problem, and the report should fit a robust model with a robust standard error and describe it as a single correction
options.misconception: merges two distinct problems into one remedy

options.text: The extreme value should be deleted as a recording error and the growing error ignored, since neither changes the coefficient materially at this sample size
options.misconception: presumes an error and a materiality claim that the data do not support

questions.explanation: Two features threaten a conventional analysis and they need different answers. The single extreme value is a leverage and influence problem: with 44 records it carries almost two per cent of the total, enough to move a mean or a slope substantially, and the remedy is an estimator whose influence on any one record is bounded, together with a report of what the estimate is with and without that record. The steady growth of the predictor with no matching growth in the error is a heteroskedasticity problem, and the remedy there is a standard error that does not assume a common error variance, since a pooled variance is estimated largely from the low-error records. The two remedies are independent and both belong in the report. What does not belong is the practice of deleting the extreme record and reporting the analysis as though it had not been there, because the reader then cannot tell whether the value was an error in the data, a case worth reporting or a modelling artefact, and those three possibilities call for different responses.
questions.hint: Say which of the two features an estimator can repair and which requires a change to the interval rather than the fit.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Writing an inference section for a design with a violated assumption
questions.learningObjective: explain how to report an analysis whose distributional assumption does not hold
questions.stem: An analysis of 60 records has a predictor that is nearly normally distributed, an outcome whose residuals fan out with the fitted value, and a standard error computed by the textbook pooled formula. The authors want to keep the same model. Explain what the inference section of the report has to say.

answer.exemplar: The model is fine and the report should say so, because a fanning residual pattern is a statement about the variance of the errors and not about the mean structure the coefficients describe. What changes is the interval, and the section has to be built around that distinction rather than around a single headline figure. Four things belong in it. First, the diagnostic that revealed the problem, with the figure or statistic that revealed it, because a reader who cannot see the check cannot judge the decision that followed from it. Second, the assumption that the check contradicted, stated in the terms of the method used, which here is the common error variance underlying the pooled standard error. Third, the corrected interval, with the correction named, and the point estimate reported alongside it unchanged, since the point estimate is not what the violation bears on. Fourth, a statement of what the correction does not do, which in this case is that it makes no difference to the small-sample reference distribution and does not address the possibility that the pattern reflects a genuine structural feature of the relationship rather than a variance problem. What must not appear is the textbook interval presented as the result with a caveat in a later paragraph, because the reader who takes the headline figure away from the report will have taken the figure the diagnostic argues against. A strong response also says what would have been better: a design that produced more records at high fitted values, or an outcome model whose variance was modelled rather than assumed, would have made the interval a smaller part of the argument.

questions.explanation: Separate what the diagnostic says about the fit from what it says about the interval, and report each.
questions.hint: A strong response names the diagnostic that revealed the problem, the assumption it contradicted, the corrected interval, and what the correction does not address.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Robustness reported as a series of alternatives
questions.learningObjective: state what a robustness section should show and not show
questions.stem: A paper reports a primary analysis and then a robustness section containing seven sensitivity analyses, each producing a slightly different estimate, the narrowest being 0.41 and the widest 0.58. The conclusion states the effect is robust. What is the fair reading?

options.text: The spread is a range over the authors' analytical choices rather than a measure of sampling error, so it speaks to the analysis and the conclusion should report the range rather than declare the effect robust
The result is robust, because seven independent specifications reaching the same conclusion is strong evidence that it is not a coincidence
options.misconception: counts reanalyses of one dataset as independent evidence

options.text: The result is not robust, because any variation at all across specifications shows the data do not determine the answer
options.misconception: treats specification sensitivity as evidence about the data

options.text: The result is robust, provided the narrowest estimate of 0.41 is reported as the headline and the widest is described as a conservative variant
options.misconception: selects the most favourable figure as the headline

questions.explanation: Seven estimates that do not coincide are information about the analysis rather than about the world, and the spread between them is the width of the choices the authors made rather than a measure of sampling error. The fair reading depends on what the alternatives were. If they vary the model within a family the authors defend, the spread shows the result is not an artefact of one specification and the conclusion is reasonably supported at the level of the narrowest figure, with the widest reported as a caution. If they vary a decision the authors cannot defend, then the spread shows the result depends on a choice the reader might have made differently, which is a different and more serious message. Either way the sentence the paper writes is the wrong one, because robustness is a claim about the analysis and not about the data, and 'the effect is robust' is read as a claim about the data. The number a reader should take from such a section is the range, and the report should say what the range is a range over.
questions.hint: Ask what the alternatives in the section have in common and what they leave out.
